name: Bradford Assay Calculator (standard curve)
seoTitle: Bradford Assay (standard curve) Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Bradford is the quickest colorimetric protein assay and the one most sensitive to which protein you are measuring. Free bradford assay (standard curve) calcul
summary:
Bradford is the quickest colorimetric protein assay and the one most sensitive to which protein you are measuring. It returns protein concentration, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts a 595 nm reading into mg/mL using your own standard curve, with the dilution factor applied. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bradford Assay (standard curve)
sections.html:
Protein (mg/mL) = (A₅₉₅ − intercept) ÷ slope × dilution factor

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
A₅₉₅blank-corrected absorbanceAU
slopeabsorbance per mg/mLAU·mL/mg
interceptfitted absorbance at zero proteinAU

Where the relationship comes from. Bradford (1976), Analytical Biochemistry 72:248–254.

sections.title: How do I use the Bradford Assay (standard curve)?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: sample absorbance of 0.48, standard curve slope of 1.05 per mg/mL, standard curve intercept of 0.03, sample dilution factor of 1 ×.

Substituting them into the formula gives protein concentration of 0.4286 mg/mL.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0.1 – 1.4 mg/mLWorking rangelinear for most proteins
below 0.1Too diluteuse a micro-Bradford cuvette
above 1.4Saturateddilute and re-read

  • Bradford binds basic and aromatic residues, so the response is strongly protein-dependent: BSA is the usual standard, but a lysine-rich protein will over-read against it.

  • Detergents above 0.1% (especially SDS and Triton X-100) interfere; so do strong reducing agents.

  • The dye binds the cuvette, so use a fresh one or rinse with methanol between samples.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Reading Bradford at 562 nm, the BCA wavelength — the peak is 595 nm.
  • Using a BSA curve for a very different protein and quoting the number as absolute.
  • Leaving the dye–sample mix to stand for different times for standards and samples.

faq.a: BCA is more tolerant of detergents and more linear; Bradford is faster and less sensitive to reducing agents. Both need a standard curve made with a protein similar to your sample.

faq.q: What does the Bradford Assay (standard curve) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns protein concentration. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.

faq.q: Does it work in both directions?
faq.a: Where the maths allows it, yes: the page states which values it solves for and which you supply. A field marked as a result is always computed, never typed into.
